entries_new.name: Hanish Islands conflict
entries_new.stopped_by: Ceasefire of 17 December 1995 and the arbitration findings of 9 October 1998
entries_new.pop: A few Yemeni fishermen on Greater Hanish
entries_new.challenge: Eritrea's offensive of December 1995 against Yemeni positions on Greater Hanish
entries_new.cost: 18 dead; 213 Yemeni soldiers and civilians captured and released three days later
entries_new.mechanism: Each state pressed its claim through licences and troops, Eritrea attacked, and the dispute went to arbitration.
entries_new.story:
The Hanish Islands lie in the Red Sea about midway between Yemen and Eritrea. In 1995 Yemen licensed diving tourism there and sent about 200 soldiers to guard a building site on Greater Hanish, and Eritrea signed an oil exploration contract for the nearby waters. Eritrean forces attacked on 15 December, and a ceasefire came at midnight on 17 December, with 18 dead and 213 captured.
France mediated. A tribunal ruled on 9 October 1998, giving the Hanish and Zubayr groups to Yemen and smaller groups to Eritrea, and keeping free access for fishermen of both countries.

sources.t: Resolving the militarised territorial dispute between Eritrea and Yemen (Better Evidence Project)
Unanimous findings on Eritrea and Yemen, 9 October 1998 (al-bab)
Brian Whitaker on the Hanish dispute (al-bab)

entries_new.name: Johnson South Reef clash, 1988
entries_new.founder: Vietnam's government, in an attempt to take possession of the reef
entries_new.challenge: China, which considered the reef its own
entries_new.cost: More than sixty Vietnamese dead, by PRIO's account; a photo caption gives 64
entries_new.mechanism: Vietnamese troops waded onto a submerged reef and planted a flag, and Chinese warships answered with gunfire.
entries_new.story: Johnson South Reef is a feature in the Spratly area of the South China Sea, near Vietnamese-held Sin Cowe island. On 14 March 1988 a small Vietnamese vessel sent troops to wade onto the reef, then submerged, and plant a flag. China regarded the reef as its own. A PRIO account, drawn from a film with Chinese footage that appeared online in 2009, says Chinese ships approached, soldiers on the reef were shot, a Chinese ship then sank the Vietnamese boat, and more than sixty Vietnamese died. It gives no separate official Chinese account. The reef is now one of seven in the Spratlys that China has turned into artificial islands.

sources.t: 14 March 1988: East Asia's last interstate battle (PRIO)

entries_new.name: AmbaCoin
entries_new.pop: More than 28,000 pre-orders claimed by its website, not verified
entries_new.mechanism: A blockchain token sold to supporters to fund a self-declared state.
entries_new.story: AmbaCoin is an online token launched in December 2018 by Anglophone separatists in Cameroon, named after their self-declared Republic of Ambazonia. Al Jazeera reported that its website called it a tradeable digital token and sold it as the Ambazonian Crypto Bond at 25 US cents. The site claimed more than 28,000 pre-orders, which could not be verified. The stated uses were funding the cause, helping displaced people, rebuilding homes destroyed by the military and defending communities. The report gives no figure for money raised, and no later status was found.
entries_new.anchor: Bamenda, Northwest Region, Cameroon (the region the movement claims)

sources.t: Cameroon rebels issue virtual currency to fund independence (Al Jazeera)

entries_new.name: Digital Kyat and NUGPay
entries_new.currency: Digital Kyat (DMMK), pegged to the kyat's black market rate; nUSDT; Tether
entries_new.challenge: Myanmar's military government, which has declared the NUG illegal and terrorist
entries_new.mechanism: An opposition government issued its own phone-based tokens to pay people and take donations outside the banks.
entries_new.story: Myanmar's National Unity Government, an opposition body fighting the military government, announced in December 2021 that it recognised the dollar token Tether as an official currency. In mid-2022 it issued a Digital Kyat, a blockchain token held in a phone app called NUGPay. Elliptic, a tracing firm, counted about 38,000 accounts and over US$11.5 million in donations since November 2023, to armed groups, ministries, township governments and disaster relief. Elliptic says use varies by region and has not been established everywhere the NUG nominally controls.
entries_new.anchor: Sagaing Region, Myanmar, where the NUG said it would base its headquarters

sources.t: The Digital Kyat: tracing the CBDC financing over $11.5 million in civil war donations (Elliptic)
Myanmar shadow government approves crypto as official currency (Al Jazeera)

zones_new.name: War fought with a stronger country's army
zones_new.essay:
Rebels who fight a government alone can lose as soon as that government gathers its strength. One answer is to fight beside the army of a stronger neighbour, called a patron. This route combines rebel-run land and an unrecognised state with a kind of force that only countries have, and it asks whether the mix holds ground longer than rebels can.

On holding ground, the record says yes. Turkey invaded Cyprus on 20 July 1974, after a coup backed by Greece's military government, and took about 37 percent of the island. The north declared independence in 1983, and it still runs its own elections with about 30,000 to 40,000 mainland Turkish troops stationed there. In Moldova, the breakaway region of Transnistria had 9,000 militiamen trained and armed by officers of the Russian 14th Army, a force of about 14,000 professional soldiers, and the ceasefire of 21 July 1992 has held. South Ossetia and Abkhazia have lasted since the early 1990s. In the August 2008 war, which an EU-sponsored inquiry said began in open form with a large Georgian military operation, Russian troops entered both.

Artsakh is the case to set against these. Armenia gave it money and military support and never formally recognised it. Azerbaijan retook much of its land in 2020 and the rest in September 2023, and almost the entire population left within days.

The cost appears in who decides. Russia supplies about half of Abkhazia's budget, the rouble is its working currency, and a 2014 agreement ties its economy and customs to Russia. Most residents travel on Russian passports. Northern Cyprus uses the Turkish lira and trades through Turkey. Some experts call it a puppet state, and others dispute that because of its separate elections. A European court looked at the same question in Ilașcu v. Moldova and Russia in 2004 and held Russia responsible for what the Transnistrian authorities did, because its military, political and economic support kept them going.

Recognition did not follow the army. Security Council Resolution 541 called the Northern Cyprus declaration legally invalid, and only Turkey recognises it. Russia keeps soldiers in Transnistria and does not recognise it either.

Each of these cases began with a people already on the land, and each patron had reasons of its own. The Kremlin endorsed South Ossetian nationalism as a counter to the Georgian independence movement. No case found involved a patron adopting a private group with no local people. So the mix beats rebels alone at surviving, and it does worse on the test of having no outside government above you.

rules.says: Treated the declaration of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus as legally invalid and urged UN members not to recognise it.

rules.cite: Ilașcu and others v. Moldova and Russia (European Court of Human Rights, 2004)
rules.says: Russia was responsible for acts of the Transnistrian authorities, because of the military, political and economic support that kept the regime going. Moldova kept a duty to use the means it had.
Demanded the immediate withdrawal of foreign military personnel from Cyprus.

odds.why: These are judgments from the record. Hold is high only once a patron's army is present, and Northern Cyprus, Transnistria, Abkhazia and South Ossetia have each lasted over 30 years. Build, law and money are low because the group first has to find a country willing to go to war for it, and no private group is on record as having done so. Recognition has stayed at one to four UN members.

own.own_why: You would get decades of safety behind a foreign army and working local courts. It falls short because the patron holds the budget, the currency and the passports, and a European court has treated its support as making it responsible for what the local authorities do. Patrons have backed peoples with a claim to the land, and a private group has neither the people nor anything a patron wants. An existing people does much better, and its result is still limited by the patron's say.

zones_new.name: War paid for by a company
zones_new.essay:
Wars cost money and mines earn it, so a company with a valuable site can look like a natural backer for a breakaway. This route combines rebel-run land and secession with private soldiers, and it asks whether company money can do what rebels and hired men cannot do alone.

Katanga is the fullest test. Eleven days after Congo's independence in 1960, Moïse Tshombe declared the mining province independent. Union Minière, which held the exclusive right to mine copper there, advanced him 1,250 million Belgian francs, about US$25 million. In September 1960 about 1,133 Belgian technicians and 231 Belgian officers and non-commissioned officers were attached to his government, and nearly 500 foreign irregular fighters arrived in early 1961. Sources differ on Belgium's position, and no other state gave general recognition. UN forces launched Operation Grandslam on 28 December 1962, and Katanga rejoined Congo in January 1963, about two and a half years after it began.

Biafra shows a company hedging. One history puts 60 percent of Nigeria's oil under Biafran control, and the British government held a stake in Shell-BP. A study of the company's position says it claimed neutrality while paying royalties to the federal government and making undisclosed payments to Biafran leaders to protect its installations. The French company SAFRAP signed deals to secure Biafran reserves. Five states recognised Biafra, and it surrendered in January 1970 after a total blockade, with about two million civilian deaths estimated. None of this lifted the blockade.

In Bougainville the flow ran the other way, because the mine sat on the rebels' land. Prime Minister Julius Chan agreed in January 1997 to pay Sandline International US$36 million to bring 44 contractors and reopen the Panguna copper mine. His own army commander had them disarmed and arrested, and Chan resigned. In 2011 former prime minister Michael Somare was reported as alleging that Rio Tinto helped finance the government's actions in the war, in an attempt to get the mine reopened. Panguna remains closed. Executive Outcomes, the most capable company of this kind, was said to count oil and mining firms among its clients, and its military contracts were for recognised governments.

The pattern across these cases is that the company wants its mine to keep working and will deal with whoever controls it. Its money pays for salaries and soldiers. It does not supply recognition, and it can draw the attention of larger forces, as Katanga did with the UN. So the mix lasts longer than rebels with no funds, and it still ended each time the state or the UN came back in strength.

rules.cite: UN Security Council action on Congo, 14 July 1960 and February 1961
rules.says: The Council called on Belgium to withdraw and set up a UN force, then authorised force as a last resort to prevent civil war.

rules.cite: South Africa, Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act 1998
rules.says: Prohibits direct participation as a combatant for private gain and requires official approval for military help abroad.
A crime, within the United States, to fund or take part in a military expedition against a country at peace with the United States.

sources.t: Oil and Biafra: an assessment of Shell-BP's dilemma during the Nigerian Civil War (abstract)
The Nigerian Civil War: foreign intervention, oil and ideology (TheCollector)

odds.why: Katanga shows money can be found when a mine already produces, so money is the highest figure. Hold is low because Katanga lasted about two and a half years and Biafra under three. A company usually pays whoever controls the site, as Shell-BP is reported to have done with both sides. Funding an armed expedition is a crime in several home countries.

own.own_why: You would get an army and salaries for a few years, as Katanga did with about US$25 million from its mining company. It falls short because a company needs a working mine and a legal market for its output, and the state or the UN can end the arrangement, as at Élisabethville in 1963. A private founder would also need an existing asset on land someone else claims.

zones_new.name: Invited in by a ruler at war
zones_new.essay:
A private conqueror has no legal title to what he captures. A ruler who is losing a war, though, can give title in exchange for help. This route combines a takeover and private soldiers with an invitation from someone who already holds power, and it asks whether the invitation makes the result last.

James Brooke is the one clear success on record. He helped the Sultan of Brunei's side fight uprisings, and the sultan's representative promised him Sarawak. On 24 September 1841, after Brooke called on him with an armed ship, the representative granted him the area around what is now Kuching. The sultan confirmed the appointment by July 1842, and in 1846 he recognised Brooke's authority without tribute. The United States had recognised Sarawak by 1850 and Britain in 1864. The family ruled for 105 years. From 1888 it did so as a state protected by Britain, which ran its foreign relations. Vyner Brooke ceded it to Britain in 1946, over the objection of his heir and most native council members.

Bob Denard shows the modern version. He returned to the Comoros on 13 May 1978 with 43 men, backed by the government of Rhodesia, and restored President Ahmed Abdallah. For 11 years he commanded the 500-strong presidential guard, became a citizen and acquired hotels and land, while other countries dealt with the president. Abdallah was shot in his office in 1989. Denard and another man were later acquitted of the murder for lack of evidence, and French paratroopers took him to South Africa. When he landed again in 1995, France was against him and the attempt lasted about a week.

William Walker was invited into Nicaragua's civil war by the Democratic Party faction and arrived in June 1855 with 58 men. He captured Granada, installed a president and held real power as army chief. Costa Rica declared war in March 1856, and he surrendered on 1 May 1857. Executive Outcomes regained the diamond fields for Sierra Leone's government in 1995, then left when that government yielded to international pressure. Sandline's contractors in Papua New Guinea had a signed contract with the prime minister, and his own army commander arrested them.

So an invitation does better than conquest alone. It gives something that other countries can treat as lawful, and Brooke and Denard both lasted more than a decade. It worked for Brooke in a place where no stronger outside power objected. In the later cases the ruler stayed the recognised government and the hired force depended on that ruler, on a foreign power, or on both. Mercenaries also now have fewer protections, and several countries criminalise this work.

rules.cite: Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, Art. 47
rules.says: A mercenary has no right to combatant or prisoner of war status. Six conditions must all be met.
Also covers foreigners recruited to overthrow a government for private gain. Most large states have not joined.

rules.cite: Treaty of 14 June 1888, Sarawak and Britain
rules.says: Made Sarawak a state protected by Britain, self-governing at home, with Britain running foreign relations and holding a veto over any cession to a foreign state.

odds.why: Hold is the best of the armed routes because Brooke lasted 105 years and Denard 11, both on a ruler's grant or favour. Law stays low because mercenary laws now reach recruits and funders at home. Recognition went to Brooke's Sarawak in the 1800s and, for Denard, stayed with the president he protected. Modern invitations have ended with the host's own army or a foreign power.

own.own_why: You would get a title that looks lawful and real power behind a ruler, as Denard had for 11 years. Brooke came close in the 1800s under a sultan's grant, and later under British protection. It falls short today because the ruler stays the recognised government and can dismiss or lose you, France ended Denard's last landing in about a week, and home countries can prosecute. It sits level with holding land with private soldiers, since the invitation offers legal cover and also tightens the dependence.

zones_new.name: Private invasion or revolt, then joining a bigger country
zones_new.essay:
A filibuster, in the 1800s sense, was a private citizen who led an armed expedition into another country. Many hoped their own government would then take the land. This route combines private conquest and an unrecognised state with a deal to join a larger country, and it asks whether the promise of a powerful new owner helps a group hold what it takes.

Texas, a revolt inside a Mexican province, is the largest success. It declared independence from Mexico on 2 March 1836, and its forces won at San Jacinto on 21 April and captured General Santa Anna. That September Texans voted heavily for annexation. The United States recognised the republic on 3 March 1837. Santa Anna, back in Mexico, renounced the guarantees he had made. Texas offered itself in August 1837 and withdrew the offer in October 1838 because Congress did nothing. A treaty signed in 1844 failed in the US Senate, 35 to 16. A joint resolution passed in 1845, the Senate vote being 27 to 25. Mexico then signed a treaty guaranteeing Texan independence as long as it stayed separate, and Texas accepted the American offer anyway. It became a state on 29 December 1845, and the transfer was completed on 19 February 1846. It had been separate for just under ten years.

West Florida went faster. Armed rebels took the Spanish fort at Baton Rouge on 23 September 1810 and asked for annexation and money. President Madison declared the area already part of the Louisiana Purchase and occupied it that December, ignoring the governor's protest about conditions. Hawaii's leaders overthrew the queen in 1893 and President Cleveland refused them, so they wrote a constitution and waited. Annexation came on 12 August 1898.

Most of those who tried did not get that far. James Long declared independence at Nacogdoches in 1819, the year a treaty fixed the US border at the Sabine River, and Spanish troops drove his men out that autumn. William Walker adopted Louisiana's civil code in Baja California and legalised slavery in Nicaragua, and the United States annexed neither place. A jury took eight minutes to acquit him of illegal war in 1854. Narciso López's men were executed in Cuba in 1851. In 1849 President Taylor had his ships blockaded and seized, and a federal grand jury later indicted him and his backers.

So this mix does far better than conquest alone, on one condition: a neighbouring country must already want the land, and it must be stronger than the current owner. The price is the whole aim of a separate place. Texas, West Florida and Hawaii ended up under American law, and the people who succeeded had asked for that result.

rules.says: Charged as conspiracy to violate the Act in the 1981 Dominica prosecutions.

rules.cite: Joint resolution for annexing Texas, signed 1 March 1845
rules.says: Offered Texas admission as a state by a vote of both houses of Congress, after a treaty had failed in the Senate.

sources.t: Texas annexation timeline (Texas State Library and Archives Commission)
Guide to US recognition: Texas (Office of the Historian)

odds.why: Texas held for nearly ten years, Hawaii for about four, and West Florida for about 2.5 months, each with a larger country nearby. Most other filibusters were expelled or executed within months. Recognition is above the plain conquest route because the US did recognise Texas. These successes all date from before 1900, and conquest now gives a state no title, so the odds apply mainly to the record.

own.own_why: You could gain a real country for some years, as Texas did for just under ten, with its own laws and courts. It falls short because the plan ends by handing everything to the larger country, and a state that annexes by force now faces refusal of recognition. A group that wanted to stay separate would have nothing to offer the neighbour whose help it needs.

zones_new.name: Seizing a platform or ship by force
zones_new.essay:
Offshore structures and ships are small enough for a few people to take. This route combines abandoned platforms and seized ships with the idea of getting a place by force, and it asks whether force at sea works better than simply occupying an empty structure.

Sealand is the main case. Roy Bates took Roughs Tower, a former British sea fort, from Radio Caroline staff at the end of 1966, lost it when his men ran short of food, and retook it in April 1967, fighting off Radio Caroline. A Chelmsford judge ruled in October 1968 that firearms law did not reach beyond the three-mile limit, after his son fired a pistol across the bow of a ship servicing a buoy. British officials then concluded he was doing no actual harm and that no force or special law was justified.

The attack of August 1978 came from inside. Gernot Pütz, lawyer for Alexander Achenbach, who had drafted Sealand's constitution, took over the fort while the elder Bateses had been lured to Austria. They retook it by helicopter, fined him 75,000 Deutsche Marks and held him for about six weeks. A German diplomat came out to check on him, which the family cites as recognition. Germany called the episode an act of piracy. That same year a Cologne court held that Sealand had no real territory, population or effective government. In 1987 Britain extended its territorial sea to 12 miles, covering the tower. It holds that Sealand is under its jurisdiction and has not tested this by force.

The Santa Maria shows a larger ship and a shorter result. On 22 January 1961 Henrique Galvão and rebels seized this Portuguese liner, and he later said he meant to set up a rebel government in Angola. A US Navy force surrounded the ship off Recife. On 2 February he handed over the ship, 600 passengers and 300 crew to Brazil in return for asylum. US legal experts could not support a finding of piracy, because the seizure was political and piracy requires private ends. That helped him personally, and he still gave up the ship.

On Minerva Reef in 1982 a group of Americans tried again to occupy the reefs, and Tongan troops forced them off after three weeks.

So force adds little. Sealand's long survival came from the three-mile gap in law and from Britain's choice to leave it alone. Violence there produced court cases, a diplomatic visit and a charge of piracy. A ship has no such gap, since it needs ports that answer to governments, and the US Navy surrounded the Santa Maria.

rules.says: Piracy is illegal violence on the high seas committed for private ends by the crew of a private ship against another ship.
A warship may board a foreign ship if it has reasonable grounds to suspect piracy, or that the ship has no nationality.
Applying the usual test for a state, it held that Sealand had no real territory, population or effective government.
From 1 October 1987 Britain's territorial sea runs to 12 miles, which covers Roughs Tower.

sources.t: Grimmelmann, Sealand, HavenCo and the Rule of Law
Piracy: a modern conspectus (US Naval Institute Proceedings, 1965)

odds.why: A small group can physically take a fort, as Bates and Pütz both did, so build is the highest figure. Hold is low because Pütz lost the fort again, the Santa Maria seizure lasted 11 days and the 1982 Minerva party three weeks. Sealand's decades rest on a legal gap that closed in 1987 and on Britain's restraint. Violence at sea can bring a piracy charge or a navy.

own.own_why: You would get a deck or a hull and your own rules for days or weeks. Sealand is the exception, and it lasted because Britain chose not to act, which the use of force does not help. It falls short because any coastal state can extend its waters over a fixed structure, and navies can follow a ship. This sits below buying or inheriting an old structure, which reaches the same place without violence.

zones_new.name: War that ends in a ceasefire line or frozen zone
zones_new.essay:
When a war stops without a settlement, the fighting line can stay in place for decades. It can leave a strip between armies, called a buffer zone, or a breakaway area that nobody has retaken, called a frozen conflict. This route combines a buffer zone and an unrecognised state with war, and it asks whether a stopped war creates a usable gap.

The strip itself offers almost nothing. The Korean Demilitarized Zone was created by the armistice of 27 July 1953 and is about 4 kilometres wide. Only two villages remain inside it, and only North Korea or the UN Command can give access. In January 2026 the UN Command strongly opposed South Korean bills that would have given Seoul authority over non-military entry. The UN Buffer Zone in Cyprus covers 346 square kilometres and has about 14,000 people in four villages, and the claims of the governments on either side continue. When police and soldiers from the Turkish-controlled north clashed with peacekeepers at Pyla in August 2023 over unauthorised construction work, three peacekeepers were seriously injured and the Security Council condemned the assault. A newcomer has no way in.

The land behind the line is where groups have gained something. Transnistria's ceasefire of 1992 set up a joint control commission and peacekeeping force, and it has kept its own government, army and central bank for over 30 years. A ceasefire in May 1994 left Armenian forces holding Artsakh and much of the land around it. The Sahrawi republic holds about 90,000 square kilometres east of a 2,700-kilometre sand wall built by Morocco, after a UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991 that promised a referendum. That vote never took place, because the two sides dispute who may vote.

Each of these shows how a freeze can end or decay. Artsakh ran its own elections for 26 years after its ceasefire. Azerbaijan took back much of the land in 2020 and the rest in 2023, and in 2026 an Azerbaijani military court sentenced former officials to long prison terms and, for five, to life. Polisario declared its ceasefire over in November 2020. Transnistria became wholly reliant on Moldova for imports after Ukraine sealed its border in 2022, and it faced an energy crisis when Russian gas stopped on 1 January 2025. In a freeze, the land remains someone else's in law, and that claim waits.

So a ceasefire does better than war alone for people already fighting, because it stops the killing and lets a government form. It gives a stranger nothing. The two sides, or a peacekeeping force, control who enters, and both claimants would treat a new arrival as an intruder.

rules.says: Each side moved back 2,000 metres from the front line. The zone is still run under this ceasefire, with no peace treaty.
Recorded disapproval of unilateral military actions against Cyprus and respect for its sovereignty and territorial integrity.
The usual test for a state: a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to deal with other countries.

sources.t: United Nations Buffer Zone in Cyprus (Wikipedia)
Reuters via Internazionale on the Baku sentences, February 2026

odds.why: Hold reflects the land behind a line, where Transnistria has passed 30 years and Artsakh reached 32 before it fell. Build and law are very low for outsiders, since only armies and ceasefire bodies decide entry to the strip. A freeze keeps the parent state's legal claim alive, so recognition barely moves.

own.own_why: A people already holding the ground would get years of quiet to run its own courts, as Transnistria has. It falls short because the parent state's claim survives and can be enforced later, as Artsakh found in 2023. A private group gets almost nothing, since the strip belongs to the ceasefire and armies on both sides would treat it as an intruder.

zones_new.name: Rebels fighting beside an exile government
zones_new.essay:
A government in exile can have a name, offices and sometimes recognition, and no land. Rebels can have land and no recognition. This route puts the two together, and it asks whether the pair can gain what each lacks.

The strongest form on record is Cambodia. The Coalition Government of Democratic Kampuchea was established with UN recognition in opposition to the Vietnamese-backed People's Republic of Kampuchea, and is listed from 1982 to 1993. Elections in 1993 brought it back into the newly formed Kingdom of Cambodia. That vote was run under UN administration after the 1991 Paris Peace Accords, and the Khmer Rouge refused to take part.

The Korean Provisional Government had the formal structure and fighters for 26 years. It coordinated armed groups, formed the Korean Liberation Army in the 1940s, and declared war on Japan in 1941. No country formally recognised it as Korea's lawful government, apart from a rival Chinese government at Guangzhou in 1921. When Japan surrendered in 1945, members returned to Korea and competed for power under US military administration. South Korea's 1987 constitution still honours it.

Myanmar's National Unity Government is the live test. It announced an armed wing in May 2021 and said in September 2022 that the junta had lost control of half the country, a figure that is its own claim. The European Parliament recognised it as a legitimate representative, and no UN member has done so. A 2021 deal kept the existing envoy in Myanmar's UN seat. In January 2025 it said it would base its headquarters inside the country, in Sagaing Region.

The Sahrawi republic has the widest recognition, at 33 to 46 UN members by different counts, and runs daily government from a refugee camp in Algeria. Morocco still holds most of the land, behind its wall. Tamil Eelam shows the order reversed. The LTTE lost its last land on 18 May 2009, and a body of Tamils abroad formed a transnational government a year later, which no state recognises.

Private versions have ended worst. In the 2004 Wonga plot, financiers meant to install the exile politician Severo Moto in Equatorial Guinea. Prosecutors said he offered US$1.8 million and oil rights. He received 63 years in his absence, and eight members of his government in exile received 52 years each. In 1981 James Mancham, the ousted Seychelles president, was directed to the mercenary Mike Hoare, and that attempt failed at the airport.

So the pair helps with money and standing abroad, as the NUG's fundraising shows. It has come back to power only when something much larger changed the situation, as Japan's surrender did in Korea and the UN process did in Cambodia. Each exile body also rested on a real claim to a people or a government that had once existed.

rules.says: A deal involving China and the United States kept the envoy appointed in 2020 in Myanmar's UN seat, and the UN rejected the NUG's attempts to replace him.

rules.cite: Constitution of the Republic of Korea, 1987, preamble
rules.says: Speaks of upholding the cause of the Provisional Republic of Korea Government born of the March First movement of 1919.

sources.t: Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea (Wikipedia)
Constitution of the Republic of Korea, 1987 (Constitute)
United Nations Transitional Authority in Cambodia (Wikipedia)

odds.why: Recognition is higher here than on other armed routes because Cambodia's coalition had UN recognition and the Sahrawi republic has dozens of recognitions. Money is helped by standing abroad, as the NUG raised US$42 million by May 2022. Hold is low because exile bodies have rarely retaken land by themselves. The Wonga sentences show the risk when financiers try it privately.

own.own_why: You would gain a formal voice abroad and something for foreign parliaments to back. It falls short because recognition went to bodies that claimed a real people or an ousted government, and the land stayed out of reach unless outside powers changed the balance. A private exile government has no one to represent, and an attempt to install one by force brought sentences of 52 and 63 years for the Moto group.

zones_new.name: War over a reef or sea feature
zones_new.essay:
Small islands and reefs have no people to resist a landing, and they can bring rights over the sea around them. Countries have fought for them. This route combines disputed islands and reefs with armed force, and it asks whether fighting over a feature gives anyone a stronger claim.

The Hanish Islands in the Red Sea show a fight that a court then settled. Greater Hanish was inhabited only by a few Yemeni fishermen. In 1995 Yemen licensed diving tourism there and sent about 200 soldiers to guard a building site, while Eritrea signed an oil exploration contract for the nearby waters. Eritrean forces attacked on 15 December, and a ceasefire came at midnight on 17 December, with 18 dead by one account and at least 12 by another, and more than 200 Yemenis captured. France mediated, and the two governments agreed to arbitration. On 9 October 1998 the tribunal gave the Hanish group to Yemen, though Eritrean forces had attacked and taken the prisoners. It also kept the traditional fishing regime, with free access for fishermen of both countries.

Johnson South Reef shows what force does when no one goes to court. On 14 March 1988 Vietnamese troops waded onto the submerged reef and planted a flag. Chinese warships approached, and by one account drawn from later film, more than sixty Vietnamese died. The reef is now one of seven in the Spratlys that China has turned into artificial islands. China holds the reef, and other claimants still dispute the area.

The law has tightened around such acts. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, a low-tide elevation (a reef above water only at low tide) counts as seabed and creates no sea rights of its own, and an artificial island is not treated as an island. In 2016 a tribunal hearing a case the Philippines brought against China found that Mischief Reef and Second Thomas Shoal are low-tide elevations, and it did not rule on who holds sovereignty over land. China took no part and said it would not accept the result.

Private parties have done far worse. Tomás Cloma declared Freedomland in the Spratlys in 1956. Taiwanese naval ships met his brother's boat that October, and in 1974 the Philippines made him sign over his rights for one peso. In 1982 Americans tried to occupy the Minerva Reefs, which Tonga had claimed a decade earlier, and Tongan troops forced them off after three weeks.

So force changes who physically stands on a reef, and only states can keep that up.  A private group on a contested feature would face several navies at once, each already claiming the place.

rules.says: Mischief Reef and Second Thomas Shoal are low-tide elevations that generate no maritime zones of their own.

Gave the Zuqar-Hanish and Zubayr groups to Yemen and the Mohabbakah and Haycock islands and South West Rocks to Eritrea. Yemen's sovereignty 'entails the perpetuation of the traditional fishing regime', with free access for fishermen of both countries.
Discovery gives only a starting claim, being nearby gives nothing, and continuous and peaceful display of the functions of a state is as good as a title.
Artificial islands are not treated as islands for territorial waters or an exclusive economic zone.

sources.t: Resolving the militarised territorial dispute between Eritrea and Yemen (Better Evidence Project)
Unanimous findings on Eritrea and Yemen, 9 October 1998 (al-bab)
Brian Whitaker on the Hanish dispute (al-bab)
14 March 1988: East Asia's last interstate battle (PRIO)

odds.why: States can hold reefs with warships, and no private group has lasted against one. Cloma's Freedomland was overtaken by a navy and then a claimant, and the 1982 Minerva party lasted three weeks. Law is very low because low-tide features cannot be appropriated and older rulings count only acts of government toward title. Money is low since no lender could rely on a place claimed by armed states.

own.own_why: You would get a rock and a flag until the nearest navy arrived. It falls short because every feature worth fighting over already has state claimants with garrisons, and in the Hanish case the side that attacked and took prisoners received the smaller share of the islands in court. Force adds danger and adds no title, since the acts that count toward ownership are acts of a government.

zones_new.name: Rebels with a digital state or currency
zones_new.essay:
A digital nation has members and no land. Rebels have land and trouble moving money. This route asks what happens when the two are joined, for example when rebels issue their own online money and ask supporters abroad to use it.

Two cases are on record, and they differ in scale. In December 2018 Anglophone separatists in Cameroon launched AmbaCoin, named after the self-declared Republic of Ambazonia. Al Jazeera reported that the website sold it as an "Ambazonian Crypto Bond" at 25 US cents and claimed more than 28,000 pre-orders, which the report could not verify. The stated purposes were funding the cause, helping displaced people and rebuilding homes. The report gives no figure for money actually raised. No country has recognised Ambazonia, and its interim government was arrested in Nigeria in January 2018, before the coin launched.

Myanmar's National Unity Government (NUG), which the junta has declared illegal and terrorist, went further. In December 2021 its finance minister announced that it recognised the US dollar token Tether as an official currency. In mid-2022 it issued a Digital Kyat, a token used through a phone app called NUGPay and pegged to the Myanmar kyat at the black market rate. Elliptic, a firm that traces blockchains, found about 2.3 trillion Digital Kyat in transaction volume by March 2025, worth almost half a billion dollars by its estimate, and about 38,000 accounts. It counted over US$11.5 million in donations since November 2023 across more than 53,000 transfers, for armed groups, ministries, township governments and disaster relief. It also describes an opposition-run online bank, Spring Development Bank.

Set this against the NUG's other money. It reported raising US$42 million by May 2022. Sales of property brought more, including about US$10 million for a Yangon home linked to the army chief. Use of the app varies by region, and Elliptic says sustained use has not been established everywhere the NUG nominally controls. The records are also public, which is how an outside company could trace them.

The mix gives rebels a payment system. It has given no one recognition, a border, or a defence against an army. Even a recognised state may fail at this, since the Marshall Islands passed a law in 2018 for a national digital currency and the plan wound down after the International Monetary Fund opposed it. No case found joins rebels to an existing online nation, so that form stays untested. For a private group with no people on the ground, there would be no township to pay and no soldier to fund.

rules.says: Declared the NUG illegal and a terrorist organisation, which is the view of the military government and not of the bodies that back the NUG.
Provided for a national digital currency called SOV. The IMF opposed it and the plan later wound down.

sources.t: Cameroon rebels issue virtual currency to fund independence (Al Jazeera)
The Digital Kyat: tracing the CBDC financing over $11.5 million in civil war donations (Elliptic)
Myanmar shadow government approves crypto as official currency (Al Jazeera)
The Marshall Islands SOV cryptocurrency, the saga winds down (David Gerard)

odds.why: Issuing a token is easy, so build is low only because the rebel half must exist first. Money is the point of the mix: the Digital Kyat moved US$11.5 million in donations, and AmbaCoin's takings are unknown. Hold is low because a payment system does not defend land. Myanmar's military government has outlawed the NUG, and Cameroon sentenced Ambazonia's interim president to life on terrorism charges.

own.own_why: You would get a way to raise money and pay people, and perhaps a sense of a state. It falls short because the money only matters once armed people hold land, which is the hard part, and neither case has brought recognition or secure ground. The Digital Kyat's donations are smaller than the NUG's property sales. A private online group has neither the fighters nor the land for this to help.

zones_new.name: Force in orbit or on the Moon
zones_new.essay:
On Earth, private groups have sometimes taken a place and held it for a while with weapons. This route asks what the same idea looks like in orbit or on the Moon, combined with private soldiers. No private group has tried it, and the reasons are worth setting out.

The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 sets the first limit. Article II says space, including the Moon, is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by use or occupation, or by any other means. Article IV has two parts. Parties agree not to place in orbit around the Earth any objects carrying nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction. On the Moon and other celestial bodies, they agree not to establish military bases, installations and fortifications or test any type of weapons. The Union of Concerned Scientists notes that this leaves a gap in orbit: there is no ban on air-, ground- or conventional space-based anti-satellite weapons. So the treaty's strictest ban applies on the Moon, and a smaller one applies in orbit.

The gap gives a private group nothing, because of Article VI. Countries bear international responsibility for national activities in space, and non-governmental activities need authorization and continuing supervision by a treaty country. US officials reviewed Moon Express's planned lunar payload in 2016 with the State Department and NASA, and looked at Article IV among other obligations. Under the Liability Convention, the launching country pays for damage, so it has good reason to supervise. A group would need a launch from a country, and that country would then answer for its weapons. No private armed group on record has had access to a launch. On Earth, 43 men took the Comoros in 1978. No one has yet stayed on the Moon longer than a few days.

Article XII adds another check. All stations and installations on the Moon are to be open to visits by representatives of other parties, on a reciprocal basis. A hidden fort would breach that, and a visible one could be inspected.

No case of people fighting in orbit or on the Moon was found, so all of this rests on reading the text. A settlement that declares independence and defends itself is the closest idea, and it remains a thought experiment because no one lives off Earth.

The private force routes on Earth rest on ground that can be reached, supplied by sea or air, and defended on foot. Each of those is far harder in space, and every launch still passes through a licensing country. So the mix does worse than a peaceful private presence would, since it adds a treaty breach for the responsible state and a reason for that state to shut the project down.

rules.says: Space, including the Moon, is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by use or occupation, or by any other means.
No nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in Earth orbit. No military bases, installations, fortifications or weapons tests on the Moon or other celestial bodies.
Countries answer for national activities in space. Non-governmental activities need authorization and continuing supervision by a treaty country.
Stations and installations on the Moon and other bodies are open to representatives of other parties on a reciprocal basis.
A launching country pays for damage on Earth or to aircraft whether or not it was at fault, and elsewhere only if it was at fault.

sources.t: International legal agreements relevant to space weapons (Union of Concerned Scientists)
Government OKs Moon Express mission to the Moon (Eos)

odds.why: Nothing of the kind has been tried, so these are judgments from the text. Every launch needs a state's licence under Article VI, and that state answers for what happens, so the law figure is near zero. Bases and fortifications on the Moon are banned outright. Build and money are low because no private armed group on record has had access to a launch.

own.own_why: You would gain distance from any police force once in place. It falls short because you can only get there through a launching country that must supervise you, the treaty bans forts on the Moon, and you would depend on Earth for supply. Force adds nothing that a peaceful settlement lacks, and it gives the responsible state a reason to stop you first.

zones_new.name: Hired soldiers plus a bought island or concession
zones_new.essay:
A buyer can pay for land without getting the right to rule it. A hired force can take power with no title. This route combines the two, in the hope that a purchase or a contract gives the armed part some legal cover. It has been tried several times, usually with money from investors.

The Phoenix Foundation of Michael Oliver, an American property developer, tried this path over a decade. In 1972 his foundation piled sand on the Minerva Reefs, and a Tongan expedition arrived on 18 June 1972 and raised Tonga's flag. On Abaco in the Bahamas, his foundation paid for a newsletter, and a plan was drawn up for a 60-square-mile free trade zone. In 1975 Esquire reported a planned rising, and it was claimed that the arms dealer Mitchell WerBell was managing and financing the movement and recruiting mercenaries. No arrests followed, and the connection damaged the group, which faded after the 1977 election. In 1980 the foundation gave Jimmy Stevens's Nagriamel movement US$250,000 for a breakaway on Espiritu Santo in Vanuatu, and one source alleged this was in return for casino concessions. Papua New Guinean troops were called in, the revolt was crushed in August 1980, and Stevens got 14 years.

Contracts written before the fighting have fared no better. A contract found in Mike Perdue's briefcase in the 1981 Dominica plot would have paid him $150,000 and made his company the exclusive agent for the island's economic development. A boat captain they approached went to the US gun agency, and arrests came near New Orleans before the group sailed. In the 2004 Equatorial Guinea plot, prosecutors said the exile Severo Moto offered US$1.8 million and oil rights. The aircraft was impounded at Harare with 64 former soldiers on board.

The Franco-Texian Bill of 1841 is a quieter comparison. It would have given a French company three million acres in return for building and keeping up 20 forts. It failed to reach the Senate. The Jameson Raid of 1895 shows a chartered company using its own force outside its land, when 500 British South Africa Company police rode into the Transvaal. They surrendered within days, and Cecil Rhodes was replaced as prime minister of the Cape Colony.

So the mix has been worse than either part alone. A long lease from a small state, peacefully held, has clearer law behind it. Bringing soldiers into the plan brought criminal charges in the US in 1981 and South Africa in 2005, and it costs the local support the plan needs, as WerBell's link did on Abaco. A contract signed by someone who does not yet hold power has no value if the coup fails.

rules.says: Charged as conspiracy to violate the Act in the 1981 Dominica prosecutions.

rules.cite: South Africa, Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act 1998
rules.says: Bars private involvement in foreign conflicts without approval. Mark Thatcher, arrested under these laws, pleaded guilty in 2005 to helping finance the coup plot.
Also covers foreigners recruited to overthrow a government for private gain.

sources.t: June 20, 1981: guilty verdicts in Bayou of Pigs plot (ABA Journal)

odds.why: Investors have paid, as Oliver's syndicate and the Wonga financiers did, so money is the best figure. Almost nothing was built. Red Dog ended in arrests before anyone sailed, Wonga's main force was stopped at Harare, and Vemerana lasted about three months. A concession signed by a coup leader has no value unless the coup succeeds, and the plotters' home laws apply either way.

own.own_why: You might get a contract that names you as the island's developer, and a few months on the ground at best. It falls short because a concession from a ruler you plan to install is worthless if the plan fails, and neighbours or the host's army ended every case. It sits below a peaceful long lease, because adding soldiers has brought criminal charges.

zones_new.name: War, then a peace deal granting self-rule
zones_new.essay:
A country may give a region special powers, or carve out a zone, as part of a deal to end a war. This route combines rebel-run land with a zone granted by the host state, and it asks whether years of fighting win more than asking would.

Three settlements give the answer in figures. Aceh's war, with over 15,000 deaths estimated, ended with the Helsinki agreement of 15 August 2005. The Free Aceh Movement disarmed, Indonesia withdrew outside troops, Aceh gained local political parties and kept 70 percent of income from local natural resources, and former rebels won the governorship in 2006 and 2012. Aceh is still part of Indonesia.

In the Philippines, the Moro National Liberation Front was founded in 1972, and the Tripoli Agreement of 1976 promised autonomy. It took until 2014 for the breakaway Moro Islamic Liberation Front to sign a Comprehensive Agreement, and until 2019 for the Bangsamoro government to take office with a former rebel leader as chief minister. The region has a parliament, Shari'ah courts for Muslims and powers to levy its own taxes. The law says it remains an inseparable part of the Philippines. The country's Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that Sulu is outside the region.

Bougainville shows how far this can go and where it stops. Its war began in 1988, with the Panguna copper mine as one key issue, and the 2001 peace agreement created an autonomous government and promised a referendum. In 2019 voters chose independence by 176,928 to 3,043. It was not binding. Papua New Guinea's parliament has the final decision, and as of 22 October 2026 it had held no vote and set no date.

In each case, the rebels gained real powers that many regions lack. Each process took decades. In each, the national constitution or parliament stayed on top, so a region cannot get past the test of no outside override, and national courts can redraw its borders, as with Sulu.

A peaceful host-granted zone sits at the other end of the same scale. Such a zone can be negotiated without any war and is offered for investment. It carries the same limit, since the host's law sits above the zone. A war adds nothing to what a private group could get from a host by asking. A government grants a peace deal to end a long fight with a people already on the land, and a private group brings no such people. If it started a war to win those terms, its leaders would more likely meet the outcome of the coups on record, with arrests and prison.

rules.says: GAM disarmed, Indonesia withdrew outside troops and police, and Aceh gained local parties and 70 percent of income from local natural resources.
Creates a parliament and chief minister with tax powers and Shari'ah courts for Muslims, and says the region remains an inseparable part of the Philippines.
Mostly upheld the law and ruled Sulu is outside the region, because a simple majority of its voters opposed joining in 2019.
Created the Autonomous Bougainville Government and required a referendum. Papua New Guinea's parliament has the final decision on the result.

sources.t: PNG MPs given two days to debate Bougainville referendum results (PINA)
PNG parliament urged to balance Bougainville independence with national unity (PINA)

odds.why: Once a deal is signed the law becomes solid and the region gets real powers, as in Aceh and Bangsamoro, so law and hold are the highest. Reaching a deal has taken about 30 years and thousands of deaths. Recognition counts only as a recognised part of the state. Bougainville's 98 percent vote still needs the national parliament, so this route has not yet produced a new country.

own.own_why: A people that fights for decades can get its own parties, taxes, some courts and a share of resources. It falls short because the national constitution and courts stay above the region, as Sulu's exclusion shows, and a government gives such terms after a long fight with a people already on the land. A private group has no such people, so it does far better by asking a host for a zone, and a war would add only prosecution.

zones_new.name: Refugees or settlers arriving during a war
zones_new.essay:
A place needs people. War moves large numbers of them, and a group holding land may offer those arrivals a home in return for loyalty. This route combines rebel-run land and settler republics with the movement of people that war produces, and it asks whether new arrivals make a hold stronger. Neutral terms matter here, since the same arrivals are called settlers by one side and residents by another.

Northern Cyprus is the clearest case on record. A 1975 agreement exchanged 196,000 Greek Cypriots in the north for 42,000 Turkish Cypriots in the south, though the number is disputed. Turkey then added settlers, a policy some scholars describe as a form of settler colonialism. Republic of Cyprus estimates from 2001 put settlers at 109,000 to 117,000 of about 200,000 people, while by 2005 settlers were no more than 25 percent of the electorate. Abkhazia shows the reverse step, with up to 250,000 ethnic Georgians driven out in the war, which OSCE summits recognised as ethnic cleansing. In both places more than 30 years have passed, and the arrivals or departures have changed who lives there and left the legal status unchanged. The International Court of Justice said in a 2024 advisory opinion on another occupied territory that occupation is temporary and cannot transfer title.

Refugees can be the force itself. Most members of the Rwandan Patriotic Front were Tutsi whose families had fled to Uganda after 1959, when at least 336,000 Tutsi left for neighbouring countries. The Front invaded northern Rwanda from Uganda in 1990. Talks produced the Arusha Accords in 1993, and in the 1994 genocide its troops drove away the militias that were killing Tutsi and moderate Hutu. Armed movements expelled from one country can also arrive in another. After Egypt pressed Lebanon into the Cairo Agreement of 1969 and Jordan expelled it in 1971, the PLO built what was called Fatahland in South and Central Lebanon, and its alliance's treatment of local people turned Sunnis, Shia and Christians against it. Israel invaded in 1978 and 1982, and about 8,000 fighters left Beirut. The Sahrawi republic runs daily government from a refugee camp near Tindouf, on Algerian soil.

Private founders have tried to recruit during fighting too. Walker's government in Nicaragua offered settlers 250 acres, or 350 with a family, and legalised slavery. Boer settlers founded Natalia in 1839, after Zulu King Dingane killed Piet Retief's delegation and the settlers won at Blood River, and Britain annexed it in 1843.

So arrivals do strengthen a hold when a real army stands in front of them. They give numbers, voters and soldiers, and they make removal harder. They bring no legal title, and they need food, land and protection the group must supply during a war. People who flee a war usually want safety, so a stranger's new state has little to offer them unless it already holds land and can protect it.

rules.says: Rejected the Northern Cyprus declaration as legally invalid and urged UN members not to recognise it.
Agreement between community leaders, under UN auspices, to exchange Greek Cypriots in the north for Turkish Cypriots in the south.
Signed to create a power-sharing government in Rwanda. Ratification later became impossible.
Occupation is temporary and cannot transfer title of sovereignty to the occupier.

sources.t: Rwanda history: the civil war and genocide (TLIO)
ICJ press release on the Occupied Palestinian Territory opinion, 19 July 2024

odds.why: Hold is helped where an army protects the arrivals, as in Northern Cyprus. It fails where the host or a neighbour turns on them, as with Fatahland. Law is low because new residents do not change title, and the ICJ said in 2024 that occupation cannot transfer it. A private group would need to feed and defend the people it recruits, so money and build stay low.

own.own_why: You would get numbers, voters and possibly fighters, which make a hold harder to end. It falls short because new residents give no legal title, and refugees come for safety, which a private group at war cannot offer. Walker offered free land and still fell within two years. A movement with its own displaced people does much better, and it still ends up dependent on a host or a patron.
